verses.text: Elijah the Tishbite, who was one of the settlers of Gilead, said to Ahab, “As Yahweh, the God of Israel, lives, before whom I stand, there shall not be dew nor rain these years, but according to my word.”
Then Yahweh’s word came to him, saying,
“Go away from here, turn eastward, and hide yourself by the brook Cherith, that is before the Jordan.
You shall drink from the brook. I have commanded the ravens to feed you there.”
So he went and did according to Yahweh’s word; for he went and lived by the brook Cherith that is before the Jordan.
The ravens brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening; and he drank from the brook.
After a while, the brook dried up, because there was no rain in the land.
Yahweh’s word came to him, saying,
“Arise, go to Zarephath, which belongs to Sidon, and stay there. Behold, I have commanded a widow there to sustain you.”

So he arose and went to Zarephath; and when he came to the gate of the city, behold, a widow was there gathering sticks. He called to her, and said, “Please get me a little water in a jar, that I may drink.”
As she was going to get it, he called to her, and said, “Please bring me a morsel of bread in your hand.”

She said, “As Yahweh your God lives, I don’t have a cake, but a handful of meal in a jar, and a little oil in a jar. Behold, I am gathering two sticks, that I may go in and bake it for me and my son, that we may eat it, and die.”
Elijah said to her, “Don’t be afraid. Go and do as you have said; but make me a little cake from it first, and bring it out to me, and afterward make some for you and for your son.
For Yahweh, the God of Israel says, ‘The jar of meal will not run out, and the jar of oil will not fail, until the day that Yahweh sends rain on the earth.’”
She went and did according to the saying of Elijah; and she, and he, and her house, ate many days.
The jar of meal didn’t run out, and the jar of oil did not fail, according to Yahweh’s word, which he spoke by Elijah.
After these things, the son of the woman, the mistress of the house, became sick; and his sickness was so severe that there was no breath left in him.
She said to Elijah, “What have I to do with you, you man of God? You have come to me to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son!”
He said to her, “Give me your son.” He took him out of her bosom, and carried him up into the room where he stayed, and laid him on his own bed.
He cried to Yahweh, and said, “Yahweh my God, have you also brought evil on the widow with whom I am staying, by killing her son?”
He stretched himself on the child three times, and cried to Yahweh, and said, “Yahweh my God, please let this child’s soul come into him again.”
Yahweh listened to the voice of Elijah; and the soul of the child came into him again, and he revived.
Elijah took the child, and brought him down out of the room into the house, and delivered him to his mother; and Elijah said, “Behold, your son lives.”
The woman said to Elijah, “Now I know that you are a man of God, and that Yahweh’s word in your mouth is truth.”

footnotes.content: Elijah stands before the King of kings with courage born not from his own strength but from standing before Yahweh. 'Before whom I stand'—those seven words carry the whole of his authority. When you know who you really answer to, speaking truth becomes not an option but an obligation.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: See how quickly the Lord replies. Elijah has just declared the drought in faith, and immediately Yahweh's word comes to him. Obedience met with instruction—this is the rhythm of trust. He speaks; we listen; He responds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord tells Elijah to hide. Not to run away in fear, but to withdraw to a place He has already chosen—Cherith, before the Jordan. Sometimes following Jesus means stepping out of public view to learn trust in a deeper place.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ravens—unclean birds in the Law, yet the Lord commands them to feed His prophet. What an image: the creatures that seem least reliable become instruments of grace. Our provision often comes through channels we didn't expect, from sources we might have dismissed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah 'went and did according to Yahweh's word.' No debate, no hesitation. He trusted that the Lord who speaks will also provide. That simple obedience—just doing what you're told—is the whole foundation of the miraculous that follows.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Morning and evening, the ravens brought bread and meat. Twice daily, provision. This is not abundance, it's sufficiency—enough for the day, requiring fresh trust each time. The Lord teaches Elijah (and us) not to store up tomorrow's confidence, but to meet Him new each day.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The brook dried up. Even the supply that was faithful cannot sustain forever. The Lord designs seasons of provision to end so that we won't cling to the means and forget the One who provides. Each ending is an invitation to move forward in faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Again, 'Yahweh's word came to him.' Not silence, not mystery—the Lord speaks clearly and continually to His servant. When you're walking in obedience, you can expect His direction to come when you need it most.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Zarephath, belonging to Sidon—Gentile territory. The Lord sends His prophet far from home, to a widow, to be sustained by a foreigner. Even in exile, even beyond the borders of covenant, Yahweh's provision reaches. And He prepares the heart that will open the door.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At the gate, gathering sticks—the widow is in her poverty when Elijah finds her. She was not waiting for a miracle; she was doing what she could with what she had. How many times does the Lord meet us at the gate, in the midst of our small, faithful efforts?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah's second request: not just water, but bread. He asks for something costly—her last meal. This is where faith becomes concrete, where a stranger's word must outweigh hunger. And she gives.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Listen to her despair: 'that we may eat it, and die.' She has measured out her last days. Yet she swears by 'Yahweh your God'—not her God yet, but she honors the God of this stranger. In her darkness, she speaks as one who knows whom to fear.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'Don't be afraid.' Three small words that reverse everything. Elijah asks her to trust first—to give her prophet his portion before she feeds her son. To feed a stranger before feeding her child. That's not logic; that's the test of faith.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The jar of meal will not run out, the jar of oil will not fail—until rain comes. The promise is bound to a known end, not to endless supply. Yahweh speaks to the exact limit, teaching us that provision is measured, purposeful, and temporary. Until the next thing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She went and did. Again, that phrase—obedience first, blessing follows. 'She, and he, and her house, ate many days.' Not just survived: they ate. And they ate together. The widow and the prophet and her son—a household knit by trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The miracle is matter-of-fact: the jar didn't run out, the oil didn't fail. Just as promised. The Lord keeps His word the way you keep your promises—faithfully, simply, without fanfare. Reliability is His nature.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Then sickness—then death. The boy's breath goes out. Just when the widow had learned to trust, when the household was eating well, the worst happens. Sometimes following faith does not prevent sorrow. It only changes what we do when sorrow comes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: She accuses Elijah: 'You have come to bring my sin to memory, and to kill my son.' In her grief, she sees the prophet as the cause, not the cure. We've all spoken like this—blamed the messenger when God allowed a wound. Her pain is real, and so is her doubt.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah takes the dead child and carries him to his own room. No words of explanation—just action. Sometimes compassion moves before the mind understands. He carried the boy out of sight, out of the house's grief, into the place where prayer could happen.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: In private, Elijah cries out: 'Have you also brought evil on the widow?' He voices the accusation the widow made, bringing her complaint straight to the Lord. This is how true prayer works—not rehearsed words, but honest anguish laid at God's feet.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He stretched himself on the child three times. Three times he placed his body on the dead boy and called to Yahweh. Desperate, physical, intimate intercession. He did not pray from a distance—he wrapped himself around the problem and would not let it go.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yahweh listened. The child's soul came back. The Lord heard His servant's desperate prayer and answered with resurrection. In a small room, before any crowd, the dead lived. The Lord's power is not reserved for public spectacles.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah brought the living child down and delivered him to his mother. 'Behold, your son lives.' The prophet becomes the bearer of good news, the one who restores what was lost. This is what it means to stand before Yahweh—to become an instrument of His mercy.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The widow declares: 'Now I know that you are a man of God, and that Yahweh's word in your mouth is truth.' Readers today hear an echo of something we learn slowly—that we know God's truth not by spectacle alone, but by seeing His word proven faithful in small corners, in ordinary homes, in the faithfulness of people who let themselves be changed by Him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
